sections.b: Chronicles opens with nine chapters of names, from Adam to the people who resettled Jerusalem after the exile. The lists are drawn from Genesis, Numbers, Joshua, Ruth and Samuel, and from other family and military records. They are arranged with purpose: the nations first (1:1–54), then Judah and David's line (2:1–4:23), the other tribes, Levi at the center (6:1–81), and Benjamin and Saul's house last (8:1–40). Short stories break in to teach the book's lessons: Er and Achar (2:3, 7), Jabez's prayer (4:9–10), the eastern tribes' war won by trust in God (5:18–22), Ephraim's grief (7:21–24). The lists end by naming their purpose: "All Israel" was enrolled in family registers, went into exile for unfaithfulness and came back (9:1–2). For a small community under Persian rule, the genealogies said who belonged to Israel and that Israel was still twelve tribes.

sections.h: Chronicles and the genealogies of Jesus
sections.b: Matthew's line of Jesus copies the form and names of 1 Chronicles 2–3 from Judah to Zerubbabel, but skips four kings to make three sets of fourteen (Matthew 1:8, 11, 17). Luke traces Jesus through David's son Nathan (1 Chronicles 3:5; Luke 3:31) and back to Adam, as Chronicles begins (1 Chronicles 1:1; Luke 3:38). Both Gospels name Shealtiel and Zerubbabel, then name descendants not found in Chronicles.

common: The genealogies of Chronicles show that the returned exiles were the same Israel God chose.
uncommon: Some scholars think the lists after Zerubbabel (1 Chronicles 3:19–24) were added after Chronicles was finished, which would make the book earlier than the list suggests.

claude.title: The stories inside the lists are one lesson repeated
claude.body:
My own reading: every story that interrupts the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 1–9 is a small version of the book's rule. Er is evil and dies (2:3); Achar breaks faith and brings trouble (2:7); Jabez calls on God and is heard (4:10); the eastern tribes trust God and win, then break faith and are exiled (5:20–26); Judah is exiled for unfaithfulness (9:1). I suspect the writer put them there so that a reader who reaches chapter 10 has already learned how to read the history that follows.

What is already in print: that Chronicles teaches immediate reward and punishment within each generation is the well-known reading of Sara Japhet and H. G. M. Williamson, and commentators note the link between Achar's ma'al and 9:1. What I add is only the claim that the stories in chapters 1–9 were placed as a deliberate preview of that rule.

sections.b: Jabez appears suddenly in Judah's genealogy, "had more honor than his brothers" (4:9). His mother named him because she "gave birth in pain"; his name, Ya'bets, sounds like 'otsev, "pain." He called on the God of Israel: if God would bless him, widen his borders, be with him and keep harm away so that it would not hurt him. The Hebrew vow is never finished: there is no "then I will." God granted the request (4:10). A town called Jabez, where clans of scribes lived, is named in 2:55.

The Talmud identifies Jabez with Othniel, the first judge (4:13; Judges 3:9), and reads his prayer as a request for Torah: bless me with Torah, widen my borders with students, may your hand be with me so that I do not forget my learning, keep me from evil by giving me companions (re'im) like myself, and let it not grieve me, that is, let the evil inclination not trouble me (Bavli Temurah 16a). The Targum of Chronicles reads the prayer in a related way, asking for children and disciples. The scribes at Jabez (2:55) were taken as his disciples.

In 2000 Bruce Wilkinson's short book The Prayer of Jabez became one of the best-selling Christian books ever, encouraging readers to pray Jabez's words daily and ask God to "enlarge my territory" by giving them greater influence and ministry. Many readers found it encouraged bold and specific prayer and trust in God's generosity. Critics, including many evangelical scholars, warned that it turned one verse into a formula, encouraged a focus on personal success and read modern hopes into an ancient request for land. Both sides agree that the verse presents God as one who hears.

common: The prayer of Jabez is a model of bold, believing prayer.
uncommon: Jewish tradition identified Jabez with the judge Othniel and read his prayer as a request for Torah learning and students.

sections.b: 1 Chronicles 3:17–19 places Zerubbabel in the royal line: Jeconiah, "who was taken captive," had seven sons in Babylon, among them Shealtiel and Pedaiah, and Pedaiah's son was Zerubbabel. Everywhere else Zerubbabel is "son of Shealtiel" (Ezra 3:2; Haggai 1:1), and the Greek of Chronicles reads Shealtiel here too. Explanations include a levirate marriage, in which Pedaiah fathered a son for his childless brother, or the use of "son" for an heir. Chronicles alone names Zerubbabel's children, including a daughter, Shelomith, and continues his line for several generations (3:19–24).

Chronicles names Israel's twelve sons (2:1–2) and then gives lists for nearly every tribe: Judah (2:3–4:23), Simeon (4:24–43), Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh east of the Jordan (5:1–26), Levi (6:1–81), Issachar, Benjamin, Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim and Asher (7:1–40), and Benjamin again (8:1–40). Zebulun and Dan have no lists; a fragment in 7:12 may be all that is left of Dan's. Judah, Levi and Benjamin, the tribes of the returned community, get the most space, but the northern tribes, exiled centuries earlier (5:26), are not forgotten. The returned community in Jerusalem included people "from Ephraim and Manasseh" (9:3).

uncommon: Some scholars think 1 Chronicles 7:6–11 was originally a list for Zebulun, which otherwise has none.

sections.b: The genealogies put Judah first and give it the most space (2:3–4:23), though Reuben was the firstborn. Chronicles explains: Reuben lost the birthright, which went to Joseph, but "Judah grew strong among his brothers, and a ruler came from him" (5:1–2). Judah's family includes Canaanites, an Egyptian, Ishmaelites, Kenizzites and Kenites, and its central line runs through Perez and Hezron to David (2:9–15).

sections.h: David at the center of the genealogies
sections.b: David is the seventh son of Jesse in Chronicles (2:15), against the eighth in 1 Samuel 16:10–11. His nineteen sons, his sister Tamar and the kings descended from him are listed in 3:1–16, and his line continues after the exile to the Chronicler's own day (3:17–24). Chronicles credits David with founding the temple's music (6:31–32) and, with Samuel, the gatekeepers' order (9:22).

Levi stands at the center of the genealogies (6:1–81). The high-priest line runs from Aaron through Eleazar, Phinehas and Zadok to Jehozadak, who went into exile (6:1–15), leaving out Eli's family and other high priests named elsewhere. The clans of Gershom, Kohath and Merari follow, with Samuel's family placed among the Kohathites (6:22–28). Only Aaron's sons offer sacrifice, burn incense and make atonement; the other Levites serve the tabernacle (6:48–49). The towns with pastureland follow Joshua 21 (6:54–81); Joshua gives forty-eight, but fewer survive in Chronicles' damaged list.

sections.h: Gatekeepers and temple servants after the exile
sections.b: 1 Chronicles 9 describes the priests, Levites and gatekeepers in Jerusalem after the return. Gatekeepers are counted among the Levites (9:26), guarding the doors, the storerooms and the key; others care for utensils, flour, oil and spices, and the bread set out each Sabbath (9:17–32). Ezra 2:40–42 lists gatekeepers separately, which suggests their status grew in the Persian period.

David appointed singers "once the ark had a place to rest" (6:31). Their leaders came from Levi's three clans: Heman of Kohath, Samuel's grandson, in the center, Asaph of Gershom on his right, and Ethan of Merari on his left, each with a genealogy back to Levi (6:33–47). In the returned community the singers lived in temple rooms, free from other duties, "at their work day and night" (9:33).

Two prayers break into the lists of 1 Chronicles 1–9. Jabez called on the God of Israel for blessing and protection, "and God brought about what he asked" (4:10). The eastern tribes "shouted" to God in battle, and "he let himself be moved by their pleas, since they had put their trust in him" (5:20). Both prepare for the book's later theme that God hears those who seek him (2 Chronicles 7:14).

The genealogies mark exile at several points: the eastern tribes deported by the king of Assyria (5:6, 26), the high priest Jehozadak taken when Nebuchadnezzar carried Judah away (6:15), Jeconiah "who was taken captive" (3:17), and the summary, "Judah was carried off into exile to Babylon because of their unfaithfulness" (9:1). The lines continue on the other side: David's house through Zerubbabel (3:19), and the first inhabitants who lived in their towns after the return (9:2).

sections.h: Reuben, Gad and Manasseh "to this day"
sections.b: 1 Chronicles 5:26 says the king of Assyria carried the eastern tribes to Halah, Habor, Hara and the river of Gozan, "and they are there to this day." Like 2 Kings 17:23, which says Israel was exiled to Assyria "to this day," it records that these tribes had not returned, here written centuries later. Yet the Chronicler still lists their families and includes northerners in the community at Jerusalem (9:3).

1 Chronicles 2 lists Caleb (or Chelubai) son of Hezron as a founder of Judah's clans, with wives and towns around Hebron and Bethlehem (2:9, 18–20, 42–50). 1 Chronicles 4:15 names "Caleb son of Jephunneh," the faithful spy, and 4:13 his nephew Othniel. Some readers take them as two men; many scholars see one clan remembered in two ways, as a Kenizzite group that joined Judah (Numbers 32:12) and as part of Judah's family tree.

sections.b: Saul's genealogy appears twice (8:29–40; 9:35–44), tracing his family from the "father of Gibeon" through Ner and Kish to Saul and Jonathan, and then about ten generations after Merib-baal's son Micah. It uses the older names Esh-baal and Merib-baal, which Samuel changes to Ish-bosheth and Mephibosheth. The second copy leads into Saul's death in chapter 10.

sections.h: Anani and the ruler from Judah
sections.b: Chronicles explains Judah's first place: "a ruler came from him" (5:2), echoing Jacob's blessing on Judah (Genesis 49:10). The Targum of Chronicles reads the last name in David's line, Anani (3:24), whose name recalls the clouds of Daniel 7:13, as "the King Messiah who is to be revealed."

sections.h: Names in the Hebrew and Greek of Chronicles
sections.b: The lists of 1 Chronicles 1–9 show many differences between the Masoretic Text and the Greek, and between Chronicles and its sources. Many come from letters that look alike, such as d and r (Diphath and Riphath, 1:6; Rodanim and Dodanim, 1:7). Others come from a scribe's eye skipping between repeated words, which accounts for missing names like Juttah and Gibeon in the Levite towns (6:59–60) and Ahaz in 9:41. The two copies of Saul's family (8:29–38; 9:35–44) let readers see how a list changed in copying.

sections.h: Ketiv and Qere in the genealogies
sections.b: In the genealogies the Masoretes often marked names whose written form (Ketiv) differed from the traditional reading (Qere): Alvah for Aliah (1:51), Zohar for Izhar (4:7), Zuph for Ziph (6:35), Jashub for Jashib (7:1), Hubbah for Jachbah (7:34), "Bani, of" for Benjamin (9:4), Jeiel for Jeuel (9:35). Most differ by waw and yod, which look alike. The King James Version sometimes combined the two, producing names such as Jezoar (4:7) and Birzavith (7:31).

sections.b: 1 Chronicles 1:5–23 copies the Table of Nations from Genesis 10, dropping its remarks on lands, languages and Nimrod's kingdom. It keeps Genesis' order, Japheth, Ham and Shem, so that Israel's ancestor Shem comes last. By beginning with Adam and all the nations, Chronicles places Israel within the whole human family.

The genealogy of Judah includes many outsiders: Bath-shua the Canaanite (2:3), Tamar (2:4), Jether the Ishmaelite (2:17), the Egyptian slave Jarha who married his master's daughter (2:34–35), Bithiah daughter of Pharaoh (4:18), Kenizzites (4:13–15) and Kenites (2:55). Simeon's clans include Ishmaelite names (4:25), and Machir's mother was an Aramean (7:14).

sections.b: 1 Chronicles 6:1–15 traces Zadok from Aaron through Eleazar and Phinehas, and his descendants to Jehozadak, who went into exile. Ezra's genealogy follows the same line in a shorter form (Ezra 7:1–5). Many scholars think the list was arranged to show that the high priests of the second temple, Jeshua and his sons, were Aaron's heirs.

sections.h: Korah's descendants as singers and gatekeepers
sections.b: Though Korah died in his rebellion, his line survived (Numbers 26:11). In Chronicles his descendant Heman leads the temple singers (6:33–37), and Korahites guard the thresholds of the tent (9:19), with Mattithiah making the griddle cakes (9:31).

1 Chronicles 6 places Samuel's family among the Kohathite Levites (6:26–28, 33–34), though 1 Samuel 1:1 calls his father an Ephraimite. Samuel's grandson Heman leads David's singers (6:33), and "Samuel the seer" joins David in appointing the gatekeepers (9:22).

1 Chronicles 5:1–2 explains that Reuben, Israel's firstborn, lost his birthright because he slept with his father's concubine (Genesis 35:22; 49:4). The birthright went to Joseph's sons, while leadership went to Judah. Chronicles thus divides the firstborn's rights in two.

The genealogies of 1 Chronicles have no list for Dan, unless "Hushim, the sons of Aher" (7:12) is a remnant of it; Hushim is Dan's son in Genesis 46:23. In the Levite towns, Dan is missing from 6:61; two of its towns, Eltekeh and Gibbethon, are gone, and the other two appear under Ephraim (6:69). Revelation 7:5–8 likewise leaves Dan out of its twelve tribes.

Chronicles spells the Assyrian king's name Tilgath-pilneser and names "Pul" alongside him as the one God stirred up to exile the eastern tribes (5:6, 26). Babylonian records show that Pulu was Tiglath-pileser III's name as king of Babylon.

In Hezekiah's time five hundred Simeonites went to the hill country of Seir and "struck down the survivors who had escaped from Amalek" (4:42–43), the Old Testament's last report of fighting with Amalek.

Saul's ancestors lived at Gibeon (8:29; 9:35), the old Hivite city whose people made a treaty with Joshua. The "servants given to the temple" of 9:2 were identified by the rabbis with the Gibeonites Joshua made woodcutters and water carriers (Joshua 9:27).
The genealogy of Manasseh notes simply that "Zelophehad had daughters" (7:15), assuming the reader knows how they won the right to inherit (Numbers 27:1–11).

Chronicles calls Jonathan's son Merib-baal (8:34) or Meri-baal (9:40), the older form of Mephibosheth, and traces his son Micah's line through many generations (8:35–40), showing that Saul's house continued in Israel.

1 Chronicles 7:20–27 gives Joshua's ancestry, ten generations from Ephraim, including Elishama, Ephraim's leader in the wilderness. His father's name is spelled Non in this verse only (7:27). His line descends from Beriah, the son born after Ephraim's grief (7:23).
